claims.claim: Pine and Gilmore introduced the 'experience economy' in a 1998 Harvard Business Review article, arguing that an experience occurs when a company uses services as the stage and goods as props to engage a customer in a memorable, personal way, and that experiences are a distinct economic offering beyond commodities, goods, and services.

Pine and Gilmore describe four realms of experience — entertainment, educational, escapist, and esthetic — positioned by two axes: customer participation (passive to active) and connection to the event (absorption to immersion).

A 'moment of truth' is any episode in which a guest contacts an aspect of the organization and forms an impression of its service quality; the ordered sequence of these moments across a visit is the 'cycle of service.' The concept is credited to Karl Albrecht (with Ron Zemke) and was popularized in service management by Jan Carlzon.

Service blueprinting, introduced by G. Lynn Shostack in a 1984 Harvard Business Review article, adds the customer's actions and the 'line of visibility' to a process diagram so a service can be designed, documented, and improved as a whole experience rather than as isolated back-office steps.

The Net Promoter Score, introduced by Fred Reichheld in a 2003 Harvard Business Review article, is derived from one question — how likely, on a 0–10 scale, a customer is to recommend a company — classing 9–10 as promoters, 7–8 as passives, and 0–6 as detractors, and computing the score as the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors.

NPS is widely used but its claimed superiority is contested: peer-reviewed work (Keiningham, Cooil, Andreassen & Aksoy, Journal of Marketing 2007) found the net-promoter metric predicted firm revenue growth no better than other established customer-satisfaction and loyalty measures.

The guest journey is commonly framed as an ordered set of stages — pre-arrival, arrival, stay, departure, and post-stay — each composed of touchpoints where the guest interacts with the operation; experience design treats the whole sequence as something to be intentionally shaped.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Net Promoter Score is a uniquely superior predictor of company growth
positions: Reichheld (2003) argued that the single 'would you recommend' question is the best available predictor of growth in most industries.
Keiningham et al. (2007) and later replications found NPS performs no better than other satisfaction/loyalty metrics at predicting growth.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present NPS as widely adopted and useful as one metric among several, and present its claim to superiority as genuinely debated in the academic literature; attribute both the metric and the critique.

sourceRecords.title: Welcome to the Experience Economy
sourceRecords.provider: Harvard Business Review (B. Joseph Pine II and James H. Gilmore)
sourceRecords.notes: Originating source for the experience-economy concept, the stage/props definition of an experience, and the four realms (entertainment, educational, escapist, esthetic) on participation and connection axes. HBR page is paywalled; verified the framework and definitions from the article's widely cited references and the author's own summaries. Copyrighted — facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The One Number You Need to Grow
sourceRecords.notes: Origin of the Net Promoter Score: the 0–10 'would you recommend' question, promoter (9–10)/passive (7–8)/detractor (0–6) categories, and NPS = %promoters − %detractors. Confirmed author (Reichheld) and December 2003 date directly from the HBR page header; article body is paywalled, methodology details cross-checked against multiple secondary summaries. Copyrighted, REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: A Longitudinal Examination of Net Promoter and Firm Revenue Growth
sourceRecords.provider: Journal of Marketing (Keiningham, Cooil, Andreassen & Aksoy)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed critique used to represent the NPS debate: finds the net-promoter metric no better than other satisfaction/loyalty measures at predicting firm revenue growth. Cited for its finding only; abstract and secondary summaries reviewed. Copyrighted.

sourceRecords.title: Designing Services That Deliver
sourceRecords.notes: Introduces service blueprinting — mapping the customer's actions alongside process steps across a 'line of visibility' so the whole service experience can be designed. Used for conceptual attribution of blueprinting. HBR paywalled; framework verified from article references and reputable secondary explanations. Copyrighted, REFERENCE_ONLY.
